title: A beggar at the door
hookLine: the soul stands like a beggar at the Lord's door (Sukhmani 20)
carry: the dust of good people's feet

cards: Some people will carry a couch up four flights alone rather than text a friend. Some will sit up until midnight with a form they don't understand rather than ask the coworker who does. Asking is hard.
It means admitting you can't do it yourself, and it means someone might say no. So it's striking that the first stanza of the twentieth ashtpadi doesn't open with a king, or a scholar, or a saint.
It opens with a jaachak: a beggar, standing at the door, asking.

teach.b: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: the humble beggar begs God for a gift. In Your mercy, give me Your Name. Then a second request: I ask for the dust of the feet of the holy.
Jaachak is a beggar, one who asks for alms; jaachai is the verb, to beg. Guru Arjan sets them side by side, the beggar begging, so you can't miss the posture.

teach.h: NO SHAME: THE BOWL IS EMPTY.
teach.b: It's an old picture in Indian devotion, and Gurbani returns to it often: the soul at God's door with an empty bowl. Here's what's surprising: the beggar isn't ashamed.
In Sikh thought the real trouble is haumai, the inflated self that insists it needs no one. A beggar has already let that go. They know the bowl is empty and aren't pretending otherwise.
That honesty is the opening. And look at what the beggar asks for. Not money, not success, not a long life.

teach.h: THE ASK: THE NAME, AND THE DUST.
teach.b: The Name, and the dust of good people's feet. That second request sounds odd to modern ears. It's an image of deep humility: to be so low before good people that you'd count the dust they walk in as a gift.
Sikhs echo it when they bow, touch the floor, or serve shoes at the gurdwara door.
Yesterday the traveler stood at God's door.
Today the traveler finds the words, and they turn out to be a beggar's words.

how: Sikhs reciting the twentieth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib take the posture of the jaachak, the beggar, asking God for the Name and for the dust of the feet of the holy.

o: a beggar, one who asks at the door
a guard who stands watch at the door
a pilgrim who travels to holy places

games.q: a beggar at the door — tap the pairs.
p: the self that needs no one
the dust of good people's feet

s: in Sukhmani the beggar is pictured as someone to pity
the beggar isn't ashamed: honest about the empty bowl, and asking for the Name.
the beggar asks for the dust of the feet of the holy
an image of deep humility before good people.
the beggar asks God for wealth and a long life
the stanza asks for the Name, in God's mercy.

games.q: you're the beggar at God's door, bowl in hand. what does the twentieth ashtpadi have you ask for?
o: the Name, and the dust of the feet of the holy.
a reward for coming so far.
games.why: the Name and the dust of good people's feet: two humble requests, from someone who has stopped pretending the bowl is full.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up like a bowl, and let one real need come to mind, something you've been trying to handle alone, without dressing it up.
If you pray, hold it in your open hands and ask, the way the beggar asks; if you don't, simply notice who you could ask: a friend, a colleague, a neighbor.

wordCard.voice: Jaachak, a beggar, one who asks for alms: in Sukhmani's twentieth ashtpadi the jaachak asks God for the Name and for the dust of good people's feet.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jaachak, a beggar, one who asks for alms; the stanza pairs it with jaachai, begs.

carryVoice: Your line: the dust of good people's feet. Asking isn't shameful; it's honest about the empty bowl. Day five hundred fifteen.
